messages.content: I have fall armyworm in my maize.
Sorry to hear that — how bad does it look right now? Roughly what share of your plants have damage, and are you seeing caterpillars still small and in the whorl, or are they large already?
Maybe one in five plants, and the caterpillars still look small.

That's a good stage to catch it at, and free measures should still work well. Drop a pinch of dry wood ash or fine sand into the whorl of each affected plant — it irritates and dries out the caterpillar. Handpick any you can see, ideally in the early morning. Keep checking twice a week, since fall armyworm can spread quickly.
How much does that cost?

Basically nothing — wood ash from your cooking fire or dry sand from around the homestead is free, and handpicking just costs your time. If the infestation grows past roughly one in five plants despite this, that's the point where it may be worth asking your agrovet about a product registered for fall armyworm on maize, and getting them to confirm the rate with you from the label rather than a fixed figure I could give you.
My chickens have been dying suddenly, a few each day this week.

That's worth treating urgently. Are you seeing anything unusual beforehand — twisting of the neck, greenish droppings, gasping, or birds going off their legs? And is this affecting one age group or the whole flock?
A few had twisted necks before they died, and it's mostly the younger ones.

That pattern — twisted necks and sudden deaths concentrated in younger birds — points toward Newcastle disease, one of the most serious poultry diseases in the region. There's no treatment once symptoms show; the priority now is stopping it spreading to the rest of the flock and to neighbouring flocks.
What do I do right now then?

Separate any sick birds from healthy ones immediately, don't sell or move any birds off the farm, and avoid visiting other people's poultry or letting visitors near yours for now. Contact a livestock officer to confirm the diagnosis and advise on vaccination for the surviving birds — vaccination is the main protection against future outbreaks, so it's worth asking about a routine schedule once this passes.
What's wrong with my tomatoes? The leaves have brown spots.

Brown spots can be a few different things, so a couple of questions would help narrow it down. Are the spots mostly on older, lower leaves or spread across the whole plant? And do they have a ring-like pattern inside them, or are they more solid and irregular?
Mostly older leaves, and yes there's kind of a ring pattern, like circles inside the spot.

That ring pattern on older leaves is a strong sign of early blight, a fungal disease that usually starts low on the plant and works upward. It's manageable if caught at this stage: remove and destroy the worst affected leaves rather than leaving them on the plant, improve airflow by not overcrowding plants, and avoid wetting the leaves when you water — water at the base instead.
And if it rains a lot this week, will that make it worse?

Yes, unfortunately — early blight spreads faster in wet, humid conditions, since the fungus needs moisture on the leaf surface to infect new growth. If heavy rain is expected, removing infected leaves beforehand helps reduce how much fungal material is around to spread. If it keeps recommending after that, a fungicide registered for early blight on tomato, applied at the rate on its label, is worth considering.
How much Imidacloprid should I use on my beans for aphids?

I can't give you a rate — it's on the product label and differs by formulation. When you're at the shop, ask them to go through the mixing rate with you from the label itself rather than relying on memory.
Okay but is imidacloprid even the right choice for aphids?

Yes, actually — unlike with caterpillars, imidacloprid is a neonicotinoid and works reasonably well against sap-feeding insects like aphids, so it's a more sensible choice here than it would be for something like fall armyworm. Still worth checking the label confirms it's registered for aphids on beans specifically before buying.
What if I'd rather not use a chemical at all?

A strong jet of water can knock aphids off the plant, and doing this every couple of days can keep numbers down on a small planting. Encouraging natural predators like ladybirds by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays also helps over time. For a light infestation these non-chemical options are often enough; for heavy infestation on a larger planting, they may not be sufficient on their own.
Why is my potato harvest smaller this year even though I did everything the same as last year?

A few things worth checking: did you plant potatoes in the same field as last season, or a fresh one? And how was the rainfall this season compared to last — noticeably drier, wetter, or about the same?
Same field both years, and the rains were about the same.

Planting potatoes in the same field two seasons running is a likely factor — soil-borne problems like late blight spores and certain pests build up in the ground where potatoes grew before, and a second season in the same spot often shows reduced yield even without an obvious disease outbreak. Rotating potatoes out of that field for at least one season, ideally two, usually helps yields recover.
What should I plant there instead this season then?

A crop from a different family works best — beans or another legume is a common choice, since it also helps put some nitrogen back into the soil while the field has a break from potatoes. Avoid tomatoes too in that field for now, since tomatoes share some of the same diseases as potatoes.
A worker on our farm just swallowed some pesticide by accident.

Get them to the nearest hospital or health facility right now — that's the priority before anything else. Don't give them anything to eat or drink, and don't try to make them vomit. If you can grab the pesticide container or its label on the way out, bring it with you, since it tells the medical staff exactly what they're treating.
It's a 20 minute drive. Should we try to make him vomit before we leave, to get it out of his system?

No, please don't — forced vomiting can cause its own serious harm, including the chemical damaging the throat and lungs on the way back up, and it isn't a reliable way to remove what's already been swallowed. The 20 minutes is better spent getting him there than attempting that. If he vomits on his own along the way that's different and not something to stop, but don't try to induce it.
Okay, we're leaving now. Anything else we should do on the way?

Keep him sitting up rather than lying flat if he's able to, loosen anything tight around his neck or chest, and keep him calm and as still as reasonably possible. Watch his breathing — if it becomes difficult or he loses consciousness, that's more urgent still and worth mentioning the moment you arrive.
maize leaves yellow what do

A few things can cause that, so it'd help to know more — is it the older leaves near the bottom turning yellow, or the newer leaves at the top? And is the yellowing an even colour change across the leaf, or more of a pattern, like a V-shape or spots?
old ones, yellow from the tip going down the middle

That pattern — older leaves yellowing from the tip down the midrib in a V-shape — is classic nitrogen deficiency. The plant moves what nitrogen it has toward new growth, leaving older leaves short first. Top-dressing with a nitrogen fertiliser like CAN, at around two 50kg bags per acre, usually corrects it if applied while the crop can still respond, roughly up to knee-high stage.
its already past knee high, too late?

Not necessarily too late to help, though the benefit is smaller the later you go — a top-dress can still support the plant through grain filling even past knee-high, just don't expect as full a recovery as if it had been applied earlier. Worth doing rather than skipping it entirely.
Is my cassava safe to eat? Some of the roots have brown patches inside.

That's worth being cautious about — brown, dry, corky patches inside cassava roots are often a sign of Cassava Brown Streak Disease, and the damage inside usually extends beyond what's visible at a single cut. How much of the harvest is affected — a few roots, or most of them?
Maybe a third of what I dug up so far.

For the affected roots, it's safer not to rely on cutting around the bad parts — the eating and market quality is compromised even in sections that look okay, and there's added risk of rot setting in on top of the disease. For the unaffected two-thirds, they should be fine to use normally.
Should I still use cuttings from these plants for next season?

No, that's the more important thing to avoid — don't take planting material from any plant that showed this disease, even if some of its own roots looked fine, since the infection can be present without every root showing obvious damage. Get clean, ideally certified cuttings from a source that hasn't had this problem for your next planting.
Something is eating my sorghum leaves, ragged holes and there's a caterpillar inside the whorl.
That sounds like fall armyworm, which attacks sorghum as readily as maize. Check how many plants are affected and whether the caterpillars are still small — that changes how urgently you need to act.
About a third of the field, and the caterpillars are on the bigger side already, maybe three centimetres.

At that size the caterpillars have usually moved deeper into the whorl and are harder to kill with ash or sand alone, since they're less exposed. Handpicking is still worth doing where you can reach them, and check the whorls in the early morning when they're most active near the surface. With a third of the field affected at this stage, it's also worth asking your agrovet about a product registered for fall armyworm on sorghum, since home remedies work best on small larvae.
What if I can't get to the agrovet this week?

Keep handpicking and checking the crop every couple of days in the meantime — it won't stop the infestation completely, but it slows how fast it spreads to unaffected plants. Prioritise the edges of the field too, since fall armyworm often moves in from field margins first.
My coffee berries are turning black and sunken before they ripen.
That's consistent with coffee berry disease, a fungal problem that's especially damaging in cool, wet, high-altitude coffee areas. Is this happening across the whole farm or mainly on certain trees?
Mostly on trees near the edge of the shade trees, less in the open sun.

That fits — coffee berry disease favours humid, shaded conditions where berries stay wet longer. Pruning to open up the canopy and improve airflow around affected trees helps, along with picking off and removing infected berries so they don't carry spores into the next flowering. In persistently wet years a fungicide programme timed to flowering is often needed on top of that, which is worth discussing with your local coffee extension officer since timing matters more than which product.
My banana plants are wilting and when I cut the stem there's yellowish ooze.

That combination — wilting plus yellow bacterial ooze from a cut stem — is a strong sign of banana Xanthomonas wilt, a serious bacterial disease. Has this shown up on more than one mat, and have you been using the same tools across plants without cleaning them?
Yes, three mats so far, and I've been using the same panga on all of them.

That's likely how it's spreading — the bacteria travels easily on cutting tools. Disinfecting your panga between plants, ideally with fire or a disinfectant, is essential from now on. Infected mats should be uprooted completely, including the corm, and destroyed rather than left standing, since the disease doesn't clear on its own and can spread through the soil and insects visiting the flowers too.
Is it safe to plant new bananas in that same spot after removing them?

It's better to leave that spot for a season if you can, since bacteria can persist in soil and plant debris for a while. If you must replant sooner, at least make sure any new suckers come from a clean, disease-free source, not from the mats you just removed.
My cassava leaves are curled and have a mottled yellow and green pattern.

That leaf pattern — mottling with curling — points to cassava mosaic disease, which is different from the brown streak disease that damages the roots. Mosaic mainly affects the leaves and reduces yield through weaker growth, rather than rotting the roots you'd dig up. Are the roots themselves looking normal when you check?
I haven't dug any up yet, it's still early in the season.

That's fine to wait on then, since mosaic doesn't necessarily mean the roots will be affected the way brown streak does. Keep an eye on new growth for the same mottled pattern, and when you do get planting material for next season, choose cuttings from plants that never showed these symptoms — mosaic spreads through infected cuttings as much as through whiteflies.
Some of my groundnut plants are stunted and the leaves look mottled and bunched up.
That's likely groundnut rosette, a virus spread by aphids that can cause serious yield loss, especially if plants are infected early. Is it scattered through the field or concentrated in one area?
Scattered, but worse near the edge closest to my neighbour's field.

That pattern fits aphid spread, since they tend to move in from field margins. There's no cure once a plant is infected, so the priority is limiting spread to healthy plants — controlling aphids on the remaining crop helps, and removing badly stunted plants can reduce the source of virus for aphids to carry onward. For future seasons, planting early in the rains tends to reduce rosette pressure, since later-planted groundnuts often see heavier aphid populations.
There's a purple flowering weed coming up all through my maize and it's really stunted this year.

That's almost certainly Striga, sometimes called witchweed — it's parasitic and attaches to maize roots underground before it even flowers, which is why the stunting shows up before you see the purple flowers above ground. Has this field grown cereals like maize or sorghum repeatedly in past seasons?
Yes, maize every season for at least five years.

That's a major reason it's built up — Striga seed can survive in soil for years and increases with continuous cereal cropping. Rotating with a trap crop or a legume like beans for a season or two helps starve out the Striga seed bank, since it germinates in response to cereal roots but can't complete its lifecycle on a non-host. Hand-pulling any Striga you see before it flowers and seeds also helps slow the buildup, even though it won't fix an already heavy infestation in one season.
I'm finding termites in my maize store, is my grain ruined?
Not necessarily ruined, but it's worth checking how much damage there is. Are the termites actually inside the grain itself, or mainly in the structure of the store — the walls, poles, or sacks?
Mostly in the sacks and around the base of the store, a few in loose grain on the floor.

That's more manageable — termites damaging the store structure and loose spillage is different from them having gotten deep into sealed grain. Raise your storage off the ground on a platform if it isn't already, since ground contact is usually how they get in, and clear any grain that's fallen loose rather than leaving it to attract more. Grain that's still in good sacks and hasn't been chewed into should be fine to keep using.
My stored maize has tiny holes all through the kernels and there's a lot of powder in the sacks.

That combination — small round holes and fine powdery dust — is typical of the larger grain borer, sometimes called the giant weevil, which is more destructive than the ordinary maize weevil because it also bores into the cob itself, not just loose grain. How long has this maize been in storage?
About four months.

Larger grain borer damage tends to accelerate the longer grain sits, so it's worth sorting through now rather than waiting. Separate out the heavily bored kernels — they're a poor bet for eating or selling — and dry the remaining grain well before resealing it, since low moisture slows the borer down. For future storage, a hermetic bag that seals out air makes a real difference against this pest, since the borer needs oxygen to survive inside the grain.
Some of my maize kernels look discoloured, kind of grey-green and dusty. Can I still eat it?

That discolouration can be a sign of mould growth, and some moulds that grow on maize produce aflatoxin, a toxin that isn't destroyed by cooking and can be harmful even in small amounts over time. Was the maize dried well before storing, and has the store stayed dry since?
Honestly the rains came early and I stored it before it was fully dry.

That's very likely the cause — moisture is the main driver of aflatoxin-producing moulds. Sort out and discard any visibly mouldy or discoloured kernels rather than mixing them with clean grain, since mould spreads and toxin can be present even where you can't see it clearly. For the rest, spread it out and dry it further before restoring, and for future harvests, drying to a hard, rattling kernel before bagging is the main defence against this happening again.
My stored beans have small holes and some have little bugs inside them.

That's the bean weevil, a common storage pest that lays eggs on the pod before harvest and the larvae then develop inside the stored bean. Have you noticed adult weevils flying or crawling in the store as well?
Yes, quite a few small brown beetles around the sacks.

Those are the adults that have already emerged and are looking to lay more eggs on any beans nearby, so numbers will keep climbing if nothing changes. Sealing beans in an airtight container or a hermetic bag stops the cycle, since the insects need air to survive and reproduce inside. Sun-drying the beans well before sealing also helps, and for badly infested stock, sorting out damaged beans before storing the rest reduces how much starts the next generation.
My onion leaves have silvery streaks and are getting curled at the tips.

Silvery streaking with curling tips is a classic sign of thrips feeding — tiny insects that scrape the leaf surface and feed on the sap underneath. Are you seeing this spread across the whole plot or in patches?
Patches near the drier part of the field.

Thrips thrive in hot, dry conditions, so that pattern makes sense. A strong water spray on the leaves, especially into the leaf folds where thrips hide, can knock numbers down and also raises humidity slightly, which they dislike. Keeping the crop watered evenly helps too, since drought-stressed onions are more attractive to thrips. If the patches keep spreading despite that, ask your agrovet about a product registered for thrips on onion, since heavy infestations often need more than water alone.
My tomatoes are developing a dark leathery patch on the bottom of the fruit, is this a disease?

That's usually blossom end rot, which isn't caused by a disease or pest — it's a calcium and water supply problem, often triggered by uneven watering rather than a lack of calcium in the soil itself. Has your watering been irregular lately, long dry spells followed by heavy watering?
Yes, actually, we've had a few days with no water then I flooded them yesterday.

That's a strong match — inconsistent watering interferes with how the plant moves calcium to the fruit, even when there's enough calcium in the soil. Watering more evenly and frequently, in smaller amounts rather than occasional flooding, usually reduces new cases. Fruit already affected won't recover, but new fruit set after you stabilise watering should come out fine.
My cabbages have small holes all over the leaves and I found tiny green caterpillars.

Small ragged holes with slender green caterpillars on cabbage usually means diamondback moth larvae, one of the most common cabbage pests in the region. Are they mainly on the outer leaves or getting into the developing head as well?
Still on the outer leaves for now, the heads look okay.

That's a good stage to catch it — protecting the head is the priority since damage there affects marketability more than outer leaf damage does. Handpicking larvae and checking the undersides of leaves regularly helps at this level, and encouraging natural enemies like parasitic wasps by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays makes a real difference over a season. Diamondback moth develops resistance to many insecticides quickly, so if you do need to spray, rotating between different chemical groups is more important here than with most other pests.
My sweet potato tubers have a bitter taste and small tunnels inside when I cut them.

Bitter-tasting tubers with tunnelling inside is typical of sweet potato weevil damage — the larvae bore into the tuber and the plant responds by producing bitter compounds around the damage. Is this showing up mainly in tubers left in the ground longer, or across the whole harvest?
Mostly the ones that had been in the ground longest, we harvested in two rounds.

That fits the usual pattern — weevil damage builds up the longer tubers sit in the ground, especially once the soil starts cracking and exposing them to egg-laying adults. Harvesting promptly once tubers mature, and mounding soil over any exposed tubers during the season, reduces how much weevils can reach. For planting material going forward, using vine cuttings from a weevil-free patch rather than replanting near an infested area also helps break the cycle.
My Napier grass has gone pale and stopped growing much this season, even though I'm cutting and feeding it the same as always.

That sounds like it could be Napier grass stunt, a disease spread by leafhoppers that causes exactly that pattern — pale, stunted growth and reduced regrowth after cutting, even under normal management. Is the yellowing evenly across the plant or more at the growing tip?
More at the tip, and the stems look a bit shortened between nodes.

That's consistent with stunt disease. There's no cure for affected clumps, and it can spread to healthy Napier through the leafhoppers that carry it, so removing badly affected clumps rather than continuing to cut and feed them is worth considering. For replanting, look for tolerant varieties if they're available in your area, since some Napier types handle this disease better than others, and ask your local livestock extension officer which varieties are being recommended currently.
My dairy cow's milk looks watery and slightly clumpy from one quarter of the udder, and that quarter feels warm.

Watery, clumpy milk from one warm quarter is a classic sign of mastitis, an udder infection that can come from bacteria entering through the teat, often linked to milking hygiene or injury. Is the cow otherwise behaving normally, eating and standing well?
Yes, she seems fine otherwise, just that one quarter.

That's a bit more reassuring, since a cow going off feed alongside mastitis can mean a more severe case. Milk that quarter last and discard that milk rather than mixing it with the rest, since it's not fit to sell or drink while infected. Cleaning the udder and your hands before milking, and making sure the parlour or milking area is clean, helps stop it spreading to other quarters or cows. It's worth having a livestock officer check her and advise on treatment, since mastitis that doesn't clear can damage that quarter permanently.
My calf has a high fever and swollen lymph nodes near the ears, and we do have ticks on this farm.

Fever with swollen lymph nodes near the ears or jaw, in an area with ticks, is a pattern strongly associated with East Coast Fever, one of the most serious tick-borne diseases for cattle in the region, especially dangerous for young calves that haven't built any resistance. Has the calf been dipped or sprayed for ticks regularly?
Not as regularly as we should, if I'm honest.

That's worth addressing going forward, but right now the priority is getting the calf seen quickly — East Coast Fever can progress fast and treatment works much better started early. Contact a livestock officer or vet as soon as you can rather than waiting to see if it improves on its own. Once this passes, a more consistent tick control routine, whether dipping, spraying, or hand-picking ticks off, is the main way to reduce the risk of it happening again.
Several of my cattle suddenly have blisters in their mouths and are drooling a lot, and some are limping.

Blisters in the mouth combined with drooling and limping across several animals is concerning for foot and mouth disease, a highly contagious viral disease. This needs reporting to your local veterinary or livestock office promptly, since it's a notifiable disease in most of the region and they'll need to assess it and advise on movement restrictions.
Should we still move them to graze as usual while we wait to hear back?

No, it's best to keep them where they are and avoid moving them, visitors, or shared equipment between your herd and neighbouring ones until it's been assessed — foot and mouth spreads very easily through direct contact and even through people, vehicles, and shared water points. Isolating affected animals from unaffected ones on your own farm where possible also helps limit how far it spreads while you wait for the visit.
Several pigs on my farm have died suddenly with high fever and red-purple skin, what's going on?

Sudden deaths with high fever and reddish-purple discolouration of the skin, especially on the ears, belly, or legs, is a pattern that raises concern for African swine fever, a viral disease that's often fatal and spreads quickly between pigs. This should be reported to a livestock officer or vet immediately, since there's no treatment and containment is the main way to limit losses.
Can we sell the surviving pigs quickly before it spreads further, to at least get something for them?

It's better not to sell or move any pigs off the farm right now, even ones that look healthy — moving animals during a suspected outbreak is one of the main ways African swine fever spreads to other farms, and selling sick or exposed animals also risks spreading it through markets. Wait for the livestock officer's assessment before moving anything, even though that's a hard thing to hear when you're trying to save something from the loss.
My goats have been coughing for a few days and a couple seem to be breathing harder than normal.

Coughing along with laboured breathing in goats can point to a few respiratory problems, one of the more serious being contagious caprine pleuropneumonia, which spreads quickly through a herd once it starts. Is this affecting just a couple of animals so far, or spreading through the group?
Just two so far out of about fifteen.

Catching it at two animals is a good position to be in. Separating the coughing goats from the rest of the herd now, rather than waiting to see if more show symptoms, is the most useful thing you can do while arranging for a vet or livestock officer to examine them — respiratory diseases in goats can move through a herd fast, and an early check helps confirm what you're actually dealing with before it spreads further.
I lost most of my flock to Newcastle disease last year. When should I vaccinate the new chicks I just got to stop it happening again?

Sorry you went through that — it's one of the most devastating poultry diseases for exactly that reason. Chicks typically need their first vaccination quite young, with a follow-up booster afterward, but the exact schedule depends on the vaccine type your local supplier stocks, so it's worth asking your livestock officer or agrovet for the specific programme they recommend in your area.
The chicks are already three weeks old, is it too late for the first vaccination?

It's not too late — starting the vaccination programme late still gives real protection, just with a shorter window before they'd be exposed to a possible outbreak compared to vaccinating from day one. Get them started as soon as you can arrange it, and keep to whatever booster schedule your livestock officer sets out from that point, since the follow-up matters as much as the first vaccination for building lasting protection.
My young chicks have bloody droppings and some are hunched up and not eating well.

Bloody droppings combined with hunched, lethargic chicks strongly suggests coccidiosis, a common intestinal disease in young poultry that spreads through droppings contaminating feed, water, or bedding. Is their litter or bedding damp or dirty at the moment?
It has been quite damp, we've had trouble keeping the shed dry.

That's very likely contributing — the parasite responsible for coccidiosis thrives in warm, damp litter. Getting the bedding dry and changing it more often is an important part of getting on top of this, alongside separating any obviously sick chicks so they're not further contaminating the shared area. This is one of the poultry problems where getting treatment from a vet or agrovet promptly makes a real difference, since it can progress quickly in young birds — ask them what's appropriate for the age of your chicks.
My beehive is suddenly empty, the bees just left. What happened?

Bees abandoning a hive completely, called absconding, usually happens because something made the hive unsuitable rather than the colony dying off — common triggers are overheating, pest problems like wax moth or ants getting into the hive, disturbance from smoke or handling, or a shortage of forage nearby. Did anything change recently, like nearby land being cleared, or did you notice pests in the hive before they left?
Now that you mention it, I did see some ants around the hive stand a couple of weeks ago.

That's a plausible trigger — persistent ant invasion is one of the more common reasons bees abscond, since they can't defend the hive from a sustained assault. Setting the hive stand's legs in something ants can't cross, like used engine oil or water-filled containers, helps prevent this for the next colony. It's worth cleaning out and repairing the hive before trying to attract a new swarm, since old ant trails and any damage can put off bees scouting for a new home.
My rabbit's belly seems swollen and it hasn't eaten anything today.

A swollen belly combined with not eating is a concerning combination in rabbits, since their digestive systems are sensitive and can shut down quickly if something is wrong — this needs prompt attention rather than a wait-and-see approach. Has anything changed in its feed recently, like a new type of feed or greens?
We did switch to a new batch of greens from a different area two days ago.

That timing is worth flagging to whoever examines the rabbit, since a sudden feed change can sometimes trigger digestive upset. In the meantime, keep it in a calm, quiet space and don't withhold water, but I'd get it seen by someone experienced with rabbits or a vet as soon as you reasonably can — a rabbit that stops eating for a full day is already a warning sign that shouldn't wait much longer.
My extension officer says my soil is acidic. Does that actually matter for my maize?

It does — acidic soil makes some nutrients, especially phosphorus, less available to the plant even if there's enough of them in the soil, and it can also let aluminium become more available in a form that damages roots. Did the officer give you a pH figure, or just describe it as acidic?
They just said acidic, no number.

It's worth asking them for the actual figure next time, since how much lime you'd need, if any, depends on how acidic the soil really is rather than a general description. Agricultural lime is the usual correction, applied and worked into the soil ideally before planting rather than after, since it takes some time to change the soil pH. It's a worthwhile investment where soil is genuinely acidic, since it improves how well your existing fertiliser is used rather than just adding more nutrients on top of a soil that can't take them up well.
My bean leaves are pale green all over the plant, not just the old leaves. Is that a fertiliser problem?

Pale green across the whole plant, not just the older leaves, is more often a general nitrogen shortage than the more localised deficiencies. Beans do fix some of their own nitrogen through nodules on their roots, so it's worth checking those — dig up one plant and look at the roots for small round nodules.
I checked, there aren't many nodules and the few there are look small and pale inside.

That suggests the nitrogen-fixing partnership isn't working well, possibly because the right rhizobium bacteria aren't present in your soil in enough numbers, which can happen in fields that haven't grown beans or other legumes in a while. Inoculating bean seed with the correct rhizobium strain before planting next season usually improves nodulation a lot. For this season's crop, a modest nitrogen top-dress can help make up the shortfall while the plants are still young enough to respond.
My maize is unusually short and purple along the stems this year, even though I planted the same as always.

Short growth with purplish stems, especially on younger plants, often points to phosphorus deficiency — phosphorus is important for early root and stem development, and a shortage shows up as that reddish-purple colour from pigment building up when the plant can't use the phosphorus it needs. Did you apply your usual fertiliser at planting, or has something changed there?
We used the same fertiliser as always but planted a bit later than usual this year, into cooler soil.

That timing detail matters — phosphorus uptake slows in cool soil even when there's enough of it present, so late planting into a cooler spell can produce exactly this symptom even with your normal fertiliser routine. It often improves as the soil warms and the plant's roots develop further, but if it doesn't ease up within a couple of weeks, a phosphorus-focused fertiliser like DAP placed near the row can help correct it directly.
The edges of my banana leaves are turning yellow and then brown and dry, starting from the tips.

Yellowing and browning starting at the leaf margins and tip, working inward, is a common sign of potassium deficiency, which bananas need in fairly large amounts since they're heavy feeders. Has this orchard been cropping for many years without much added back to the soil?
Yes, it's an old stand, probably ten years without much fertiliser.

That fits — potassium gets depleted from continuous banana production if it isn't replenished, since the crop removes a lot of it with each bunch harvested. Returning crop residues like old leaves and pseudostems to the base of the mat instead of removing them helps recycle some potassium, and adding a potassium-rich fertiliser or well-composted manure around the mats gives a more direct boost. It usually takes a season or two of consistent feeding to fully correct a deficiency this established.
My farm is on a slope and I'm losing topsoil every time it rains hard. What can I do that doesn't cost much?

Sloped land losing soil in heavy rain is a common and serious problem, but there are low-cost ways to slow it. Planting grass strips or hedgerows along the contour of the slope, rather than up and down it, physically slows water and traps soil as it moves. Do you know roughly how steep the slope is, and is anything currently planted along the contour?
Fairly steep, and no, everything is planted straight up and down the hill right now.

That planting direction is likely making the erosion worse than it needs to be, since water runs straight down between the rows instead of being slowed. Switching to planting along the contour, even without formal terracing, makes an immediate difference, and adding a simple contour trench or a line of grass or shrubs below your cultivated area catches soil that starts to move. Terracing is more effective still but takes more labour to establish, so contour planting is a reasonable first step while you plan for that.
Is it worth building terraces on my hillside plot, or is that only for big farms?

It's worth considering even on a small plot, especially if you're already losing soil or seeing crop yields drop on the upper parts of the slope. The main cost is labour rather than money if you're building simple bench terraces by hand, which makes it accessible even without capital, though it does take real time to construct properly. Roughly how large is the plot you're thinking about?
About half an acre, and it's just me and my wife doing the work.

For half an acre with two people, it's a realistic project done gradually rather than all at once — building one or two terraces a season, starting from the bottom of the slope and working up, spreads the labour out. The payoff usually shows over a few seasons as soil stays put and yields on the terraced sections stabilise, rather than as an immediate jump, so it's more of a long-term investment in the land than a quick fix.
Someone told me to plant mucuna as a cover crop. What does it actually do for my soil?

Mucuna, sometimes called velvet bean, is a legume grown mainly to improve soil rather than to harvest and sell, though the beans are edible after proper processing. Like other legumes, it fixes nitrogen from the air into the soil through root nodules, and its dense, fast-growing vines smother weeds and add a lot of organic matter when it's cut and left to decompose. Are you thinking of using it during your off-season, or intercropped with a main crop?
Off-season, the field would otherwise sit bare for a few months.

That's a good use for it — a bare field between seasons loses soil to erosion and doesn't build fertility, whereas mucuna covers the ground, protects it from rain impact, and adds nitrogen and organic matter by the time you're ready to plant your main crop again. Just be aware it grows aggressively, so you'll need to slash or turn it in before it sets too much seed, or it can become its own weed problem in future seasons.
Does planting beans between my maize rows actually help, or does it just compete with the maize?

Done well, it helps more than it competes, mainly because beans fix their own nitrogen rather than drawing heavily on what the maize needs, and the two crops have different growth habits that let them share space reasonably efficiently. The main risk is planting too densely, where the beans do start competing for light and water. How are you currently spacing the two crops?
Honestly I've just been planting beans wherever there's a gap, no real spacing plan.

That's probably where competition creeps in — beans planted right against maize stems or in every available gap can crowd both crops. Giving the beans a bit of deliberate spacing from the maize row, rather than filling every gap, usually gets you the soil and pest benefits of intercropping without much yield loss on either crop. It also makes weeding and harvesting more manageable than a completely mixed stand.
Is it better to put manure on my field now, right before planting, or does timing not matter much?

Timing does matter, mainly because of how long manure takes to break down and how it affects your crop. Fresh manure applied right before planting can actually harm young seedlings, partly through heat as it decomposes and partly through nitrogen being temporarily tied up rather than available to the plant. Is the manure you have fresh, or has it been sitting and composting for a while?
It's fairly fresh, only a couple of weeks old from the cattle.

With manure that fresh, it's better to apply it several weeks to a couple of months before planting if you can, so it has time to break down and stabilise before roots are growing into it. If your planting date doesn't allow that lead time this season, composting it further before use, or applying it and waiting as long as possible before sowing, reduces the risk of seedling damage compared to putting fresh manure straight into the planting furrow.
My compost pile isn't heating up or breaking down, it's just sitting there.
A compost pile that stays cool and doesn't break down usually has a moisture or airflow problem. Is the pile dry and crumbly when you dig into it, or wet and compacted?
Pretty dry actually, we haven't had much rain and I haven't been watering it.

That's likely your main issue — the microbes that break down compost need moisture to stay active, similar to a damp sponge rather than dry or soaking wet. Watering the pile as you turn it, aiming for that damp-sponge feel throughout rather than just on the surface, should get it heating up again within a week or so if the mix of materials is otherwise reasonable. Turning it at the same time helps mix in the moisture evenly and gets air back into the centre of the pile.
I've heard of zai pits for growing crops in dry areas. Are they worth digging by hand?

Zai pits can be worth the labour, especially in dry areas with unreliable rainfall, because they concentrate both water and nutrients right where the seed is planted, rather than letting scarce rain run off across the surface. The pits are usually filled partly with manure or compost, which also feeds the crop directly at the root zone. How dry is your area typically, and is this for a small plot or a larger field?
Quite dry, we often go weeks without rain in the growing season, and it would be about a quarter acre.

For an area that dry, zai pits are a reasonable investment of labour, since the water-harvesting effect matters most exactly where rainfall is scarce and unreliable. A quarter acre by hand is a manageable size to start with, even though digging that many pits properly takes real time upfront — most people find the yield improvement in a dry season justifies it, though in an unusually wet season the advantage is smaller since there's less scarce water to concentrate.
Is drip irrigation worth the cost for a small tomato plot, or should I stick to watering by hand?

It depends a lot on your water source and how much time hand watering currently takes you. Drip irrigation uses water more efficiently than hand watering or overhead methods, and it also keeps water off the leaves, which helps with some fungal diseases that spread in wet foliage. How large is the plot, and is water something you're currently paying for or hauling by hand?
About a tenth of an acre, and I'm hauling water by hand from a borehole, it takes hours.

At that scale, with hand-hauled water taking hours, drip irrigation is likely worth it even on a tight budget — a basic gravity-fed drip kit doesn't need much pressure and can cut both the water used and the time spent significantly. The upfront cost of tubing and drippers is the main barrier, but for tomatoes specifically, the drier leaves from drip rather than overhead watering can also mean fewer fungal problems, which adds a yield benefit on top of the time saved.
Does mulching my vegetables actually make a difference, or is it just extra work for nothing?

It genuinely makes a difference, mainly by slowing evaporation from the soil surface and suppressing weeds that would otherwise compete for the same water. What are you using, or thinking of using, as mulch?
Just dry grass and maize stalks I already have lying around.

That's a good, free option — dry grass and old stalks work well as mulch, and using material you already have means it costs nothing beyond the labour of spreading it. Lay it a few centimetres thick around the base of the plants, leaving a small gap right at the stem to avoid trapping moisture against it and encouraging rot. Over a season it also breaks down and adds a bit of organic matter to the soil, so it pays back in more than just water savings.
My maize keeps failing in the dry years. Should I switch to sorghum instead?

Sorghum is generally more drought-tolerant than maize, so if dry years are becoming the main pattern rather than an occasional bad season, it's a reasonable crop to bring into your rotation, even if not a full replacement. How many of the last several seasons would you say were noticeably dry?
Three out of the last four, only one was a normal rainy season.

With that pattern, relying entirely on maize is a real risk each season. Rather than switching completely, many farmers in similarly dry-prone areas split their land between the two, keeping some maize for the seasons that do get good rain while using sorghum as the more reliable fallback on at least part of the plot. That spreads the risk rather than betting everything on one crop's performance in an uncertain climate.
How big a rainwater tank do I need to get through the dry season for my vegetable garden?

That depends on quite a few things I don't have enough information to calculate confidently — the size of your garden, how much rain typically falls and over what months, your roof catchment area if you're harvesting from a roof, and how much you're watering per week. Rather than me guessing at a tank size, it's worth asking a local water or agricultural extension officer who knows the rainfall pattern in your specific area, since getting this wrong either wastes money on an oversized tank or leaves you short partway through the dry season.
Is there at least a rough way I can estimate it myself?

A reasonable starting approach is to track how much water your garden actually uses per week during the driest part of the year you can remember, then multiply that by how many weeks you'd need the tank to cover without any rain at all. It's rough, but it grounds the estimate in your actual usage rather than a generic figure that might not fit your garden's size or your local dry season length.
My new borehole water tastes a bit salty. Is it okay to use for irrigating my vegetables?

Salty borehole water is genuinely something to be cautious with for irrigation, since salt-sensitive vegetables can show stunted growth or leaf scorch if watered with water that's too saline over time, and repeated use can also gradually build up salt in the soil itself. Has the water been tested, or is 'a bit salty' just based on taste?
Just based on taste, we haven't had it tested.

It's worth getting an actual water test done before relying on it heavily for irrigation, since taste alone doesn't tell you the salinity level precisely enough to know which crops it's safe for. In the meantime, more salt-tolerant crops tend to handle borderline water better than sensitive ones like most leafy vegetables, and watering enough to flush salts below the root zone rather than just wetting the surface reduces buildup in the soil, but that uses more water, which may not suit every situation.
How do I know if my maize is dry enough to store safely?

The clearest sign without equipment is how the kernels behave — well-dried maize kernels are hard and give a distinct rattling, cracking sound when you shake a cob or handful, rather than a dull thud. Biting a kernel should meet real resistance rather than dent easily. Have you been drying yours on raised racks or mats, or straight on the ground?
On mats, but honestly the weather has been cloudy so I'm not sure it's fully dry.

Cloudy drying weather is a real risk for underdrying, since it takes noticeably longer than full sun even if the maize looks dry on the outside. If you're unsure, it's safer to dry it a few more days than to store it too early — moisture trapped in kernels that look dry on the surface is exactly what leads to mould and the toxins that come with it once bagged. If you have access to a moisture meter through an extension office or cooperative, that removes the guesswork entirely.
Are groundnuts more risky for aflatoxin than maize, or about the same?

Groundnuts are actually considered higher risk than maize for aflatoxin in many contexts, partly because the pods develop underground in direct contact with soil-dwelling mould, and partly because groundnuts are often left in the field to dry longer than is ideal. Are you currently drying yours in the ground, pulled and stacked, or spread out after lifting?
We usually leave the whole plant stacked in the field for a couple of weeks after pulling.

That's a common practice, but the longer pods sit in contact with damp soil or ground moisture during that stacking period, the more risk builds. Where possible, lifting the pods off the ground onto a raised rack or tarpaulin to finish drying, rather than leaving them in direct soil contact, reduces mould exposure. Shelling and further drying promptly once the pods are reasonably dry, rather than storing them still in the shell for a long stretch, also helps limit how much mould has a chance to establish.
My stored onions are going soft and rotting from the neck downward. What's causing that?

Softening and rot starting at the neck of stored onions is often linked to the bulbs not being cured properly before storage — curing lets the neck tissue dry and seal, and without that the neck stays a weak point where rot organisms get in. Did you cure the onions, drying them with tops on for a period before storing, or go straight from harvest to storage?
We harvested and stored them within a couple of days, no real curing period.

That's very likely the main cause. For future harvests, curing onions for a couple of weeks in a warm, dry, well-ventilated spot before storage, ideally with the tops still attached, lets the neck close up properly and dramatically reduces this kind of rot. For what's already stored and starting to soften, sorting through regularly and using or selling the softening ones first, rather than leaving them to spread rot to firmer neighbours, limits your losses on the batch you already have.
My stored potatoes are turning green and starting to sprout even though I haven't planted them.

Both greening and sprouting usually come down to light and warmth exposure during storage — potatoes exposed to light produce a green pigment along with a bitter compound, and warmer storage temperatures encourage sprouting even without light. Where and how are you storing them at the moment?
In sacks in a corner of the kitchen, so there's some light and it's fairly warm from cooking.

That's a fairly common setup, but it's working against you here — moving them to a dark, cool, well-ventilated spot, away from direct light and away from heat sources like a cooking area, slows both problems considerably. Any potatoes that have already turned notably green should have the green parts cut away generously before eating, since that's where the bitter compound concentrates, and heavily sprouted ones are best used soon rather than left to keep sprouting further.
How do I know when to harvest my bananas so they're ripe by the time they reach the market three days away?

Bananas are usually harvested green and ripen afterward, so the goal is judging how mature the fingers are at harvest, not waiting for any yellow colour in the field. A common sign of good harvest maturity is when the fingers have become rounded and lost their sharp angular edges, rather than staying flat-sided. How are your bunches looking right now, angular or fairly rounded already?
Some fingers are rounded, others in the same bunch still look angular.

Uneven ripening within a bunch is normal, so go by the more mature fingers on the bunch as your guide rather than waiting for every single one to round out, since the less mature ones will still ripen after harvest even if slightly behind. Given a three-day journey to market, harvesting at that mostly-rounded stage should put them at a good selling ripeness on arrival, whereas waiting for full field ripeness risks them being overripe or damaged by the time they get there.
My milk keeps going sour before I can sell it in the morning, even though I milk fresh in the evening.

Milk souring overnight before it even reaches the buyer usually comes down to temperature — bacteria that spoil milk multiply fast at warm temperatures, so how it's handled between milking and sale matters a lot. How are you storing it overnight right now?
Just in the container, room temperature, no cooling.

That's almost certainly the main issue — without any cooling, milk left overnight at room temperature gives bacteria hours to multiply well before morning. If a fridge isn't available, even placing the container in a basin of cool water, ideally changed periodically, or storing it in the coolest part of the house away from any heat source, slows spoilage noticeably compared to open room temperature. If you're near a cooperative with a chilling plant, delivering milk there as soon as possible after milking rather than holding it overnight at home is generally the more reliable fix.
How long can I keep eggs before they're too old to sell as fresh?

Fresh eggs stored properly, in a cool spot out of direct sun, generally hold reasonable quality for a couple of weeks, though they do gradually lose freshness as time passes rather than becoming unsafe at a specific cutoff. A simple way to check an individual egg's freshness is to place it in water — a fresh egg sinks and lies flat, while an older egg with a larger internal air pocket starts to float or stand upright. Are you storing yours at room temperature or somewhere cooler?
Room temperature, in a tray on the counter.

Room temperature storage shortens how long they stay good compared to a cool, shaded spot, so if you're not selling them quickly, moving the tray somewhere cooler helps extend usable freshness. For eggs you're planning to sell, the float test before selling a batch is a quick way to catch and remove any that have aged past a sellable point, without needing to crack each one open to check.
I keep hearing drip irrigation pays for itself. Is that actually true for someone with less than an acre?

It can be true, but it depends heavily on what you're currently doing without it and what you're growing. If you're already watering efficiently by hand and growing a low-value crop, the payback period stretches out and might not be worth it on a small plot. If you're growing something higher-value like tomatoes or peppers and currently losing a lot of water to evaporation or uneven watering, the case is stronger. What are you growing, and what's your current watering method?
Tomatoes, and right now I'm just watering with a bucket, unevenly, whenever I have time.

For tomatoes specifically, with bucket watering that's already uneven, drip irrigation tends to pay off reasonably quickly on even a small plot, both through better water use and through steadier moisture reducing problems like blossom end rot and some fungal diseases that uneven watering can worsen. The main hurdle is the upfront cost of the kit rather than ongoing running costs, so it's worth comparing prices from a few suppliers, since a simple gravity-fed system for under an acre doesn't need to be expensive to be effective.
Is it worth buying a chaff cutter for my two dairy cows, or is that only worth it for bigger herds?

For just two cows, it's a closer call than it would be for a bigger herd, since the machine's cost is spread over less milk production to justify it. The main benefit of a chaff cutter is that cutting fodder into shorter pieces reduces wastage and can improve how much the cows actually eat versus leaving stalky bits behind. How much time are you currently spending preparing fodder by hand, and is wastage a noticeable problem?
A fair bit of time actually, maybe an hour a day, and yes there's quite a bit of stalk left over that they don't eat.

With that much time spent and noticeable wastage, a chaff cutter is more likely to be worth it even for just two cows, since the time saved and the reduction in wasted fodder both have real value even at a small scale. If buying one outright feels like a stretch, some areas have chaff cutters available through farmer groups or cooperatives on a shared or hire basis, which can let you get the benefit without the full upfront cost.
Is it actually worth buying new hybrid maize seed every season, or can I save seed from my harvest like I do with beans?

This is one of the clearer cases where the answer differs by crop type. Hybrid maize seed is produced by crossing two specific parent lines, and the useful traits of that cross — like higher yield or disease tolerance — don't reliably carry through to seed saved from the harvest, since the next generation doesn't breed true. Beans, by contrast, are usually open-pollinated varieties where saved seed performs consistently season to season. Have you noticed a yield drop in past seasons when you tried saving hybrid maize seed?
Yes actually, a couple of years ago I saved some and the yield was noticeably worse.

That matches what you'd expect from planting saved hybrid seed — it's a common experience, and it's the main reason buying fresh hybrid seed each season is generally worth the cost despite feeling like an avoidable expense, since the yield gap from saved seed usually costs more than the seed itself would have. If cost is the real barrier, an open-pollinated maize variety is a reasonable middle ground, since its seed can be saved and replanted without that same yield penalty, even though it may not match a good hybrid's peak yield.
Is switching entirely to manure and compost instead of buying fertiliser actually going to save me money?

It can reduce cash spending, but it's worth being realistic about what it takes to get there. Manure and compost usually need to be applied in much larger quantities than synthetic fertiliser to supply the same amount of nutrients, so the labour and transport involved can be substantial, especially if you don't have your own livestock producing manure on-site. Do you have your own animals producing manure, or would you need to source it elsewhere?
I'd have to buy it in from a nearby farm and transport it myself.

In that case, the savings are less clear-cut than they might first appear, since you'd be trading a fertiliser cost for a manure purchase plus transport and labour cost, and the nutrient content of bought-in manure varies a lot depending on how it was stored. A blended approach — using manure or compost for the organic matter and slow, steady soil-building benefits it brings, alongside some synthetic fertiliser for a more predictable nutrient supply — often works out more practically than trying to replace one entirely with the other.
Maize prices are low right now just after harvest. Should I sell now or store it and wait for prices to rise?

Prices are typically lowest right after harvest because everyone is selling at once, and they often do rise over the following months as supply tightens, so storing can pay off if you're able to store safely and don't urgently need the cash now. How confident are you in your storage — is it well-dried grain in a good store, or something you're less sure about?
Storage is decent, I've got proper sacks and a raised platform, but I do need some cash soon for school fees.

That changes the calculation — a price rise later doesn't help if you need cash now and would have to sell in a rush anyway or borrow at a cost. A reasonable middle path many farmers use is selling only what covers the immediate need now, at the lower price, and holding back the rest in your decent storage to sell later when prices have typically recovered, rather than an all-or-nothing choice between selling everything now or waiting on everything.
My maize has holes in the leaves and I'm treating it for fall armyworm.

That's a reasonable first guess since fall armyworm is common and causes exactly that kind of leaf damage. To confirm before you commit to a treatment plan, are the caterpillars greenish to brown with a pale inverted Y marking on the head, and are they mostly in the whorl at the top of the plant?
Actually I already looked closely, they're pinkish and I'm finding them lower down in the stem, not the whorl, and some plants have a dead central shoot.

That changes things — pinkish larvae boring into the lower stem, with a dead central shoot known as deadheart, points to stem borer rather than fall armyworm, and they need different handling. Since the larvae are inside the stem rather than exposed in the whorl, surface treatments like ash in the whorl won't reach them effectively. Removing and destroying badly affected stems with deadheart helps reduce the population before they complete their lifecycle, and it's worth asking your agrovet specifically about stem borer control for maize rather than fall armyworm products, since the two aren't always the same.
My cow has a high fever and is off her feed. Given the season, could this be East Coast Fever from ticks?

That's a sensible thing to consider given how common tick-borne disease is, though I'd want to check the tick angle before assuming that's the cause. Have you been finding ticks on your cattle recently?
Actually no, we're in quite a dry, dusty area and I can't remember ever seeing a tick on this farm.

That's useful to know and does make East Coast Fever less likely, since it depends on the specific tick species that carries it being present and feeding on the animal. In a dry area without ticks, it's worth considering other causes of fever and appetite loss — general infections, heat stress, or something in feed or water are all more plausible starting points than a tick-borne disease you haven't observed evidence of. A vet examining her directly will be able to narrow this down far better than guessing from symptoms alone, especially once tick exposure is ruled out as the obvious lead.
I'm applying two bags of DAP per acre for my maize like you'd usually suggest.

That's a reasonable amount for many soils, though it can vary somewhat depending on how depleted your particular soil is in phosphorus. Has a soil test ever been done on this field, or is this based on general practice in your area?
Actually, my soil was tested last year and it came back quite low in phosphorus specifically, the officer recommended going a bit higher than that for this field.

Then it's worth following that specific recommendation rather than the general figure — a soil test result for your actual field is far more reliable than a generic rate, especially when it's flagged a particular nutrient as notably low. Since your soil was tested as low in phosphorus, the higher rate the officer suggested is the more appropriate one for this field, and it's worth keeping that test result on hand to guide fertiliser choices for a few seasons until conditions change enough to warrant retesting.
You mentioned vaccinating against Newcastle disease. I read online it should be every three months, but our vet said twice a year is enough for our flock.

Vaccination schedules for Newcastle disease do vary by vaccine type, flock size, and local disease pressure, so there isn't one universal answer — a vet who knows your specific flock and the disease situation in your area is in a much better position to set that schedule than a general figure from somewhere online. Since your vet examined your situation directly and recommended twice a year, that's the more trustworthy guidance to follow here rather than a generic online recommendation that may be describing a different vaccine type or a higher-risk area.
My tomato leaves have brown spots with rings inside them, sounds like early blight from what you told someone else.

The ring pattern is a good sign to check, but a couple more details would help confirm it's actually early blight rather than something else with a similar look. Are the spots mostly on the older, lower leaves, and do you see any yellowing around the spots?
Actually now that I look closer, there's no yellow halo, and the spots feel a bit greasy or water-soaked rather than dry, and there are some angular spots on the leaves too.

That greasy, water-soaked texture with angular spots is actually more typical of bacterial spot than early blight — bacterial infections often have that wet appearance, while early blight tends to look drier with more defined concentric rings and often a yellow halo. Since this looks bacterial rather than fungal, the approach differs somewhat: avoid handling wet plants since bacteria spread easily on wet leaves and hands, remove badly affected leaves, and avoid overhead watering, since fungicides that work on early blight generally won't help against a bacterial problem.
Someone told me salty water is fine to make him vomit after swallowing that pesticide, that's how we've always handled it.

I'd strongly push back on that, even though it's a common belief — making someone vomit, whether with salt water or any other method, isn't safe after swallowing a pesticide, since it can cause the chemical to burn the throat and airway further on the way back up, and it isn't a reliable way to clear what's already been swallowed. This holds regardless of how it's traditionally been handled, since it's about the physical harm forcing vomiting can cause, not a difference of opinion on method. Getting him to a hospital or health facility as fast as possible, without inducing vomiting, is the safer path, and that's true even for a longer drive.
Actually, I don't think rotating out of potatoes matters — I heard blight spores can't survive in the soil once the plants are gone.

I'd gently disagree with that — some of the organisms behind common potato problems, including certain blight pathogens, can persist in soil and leftover plant debris between seasons, not just on living plants, which is exactly why continuous potato cropping in the same field tends to build up disease pressure over time rather than staying constant. It's a reasonable thing to have heard, since not every soil pathogen behaves this way, but for potatoes specifically the buildup in repeatedly cropped fields is well documented enough that rotation is still worth doing rather than skipping.
My sukuma wiki has these white cottony bugs on the underside of the leaves, tell me what to do.

White, cottony-looking insects on the underside of leaves usually means mealybugs, which cluster and feed on sap, weakening the plant over time. Are you seeing them mainly on the leaf veins and stem joints?
Actually wait, I misspoke, this is my cabbage not sukuma wiki, and looking again they're more waxy white and fly up in a little cloud when I touch the leaf.

That changes the identification — insects that fly up in a small cloud when disturbed, rather than staying put like mealybugs, are more likely whitefly, which is common on cabbage and related crops. Whitefly feed on the underside of leaves too, but the flying-up behaviour and the more uniform tiny white appearance are the giveaway. A strong water spray to knock numbers down, along with yellow sticky traps placed near the crop to catch adults, are reasonable non-chemical steps to start with on cabbage.
My goats have been scratching a lot and losing wool around the neck.

Losing wool is worth a closer look, though goats don't typically grow wool the way sheep do, so I want to make sure I've got the right animal before suggesting causes — could you double check whether these are goats or sheep?
You're right, sorry, these are actually my sheep, not goats, my mistake.

No problem, that's an important distinction here. Scratching combined with wool loss around the neck in sheep is often linked to external parasites like lice or mites, sometimes worsened by wool that's gotten dirty or matted and irritating the skin further. Checking the skin closely in the affected area for small moving insects or scabby patches will help confirm whether it's a parasite problem, and a vet or livestock officer can advise on the right treatment once that's confirmed, since lice and mites aren't handled identically.
My citrus tree has small green insects clustering on new shoots, I've been told it's aphids.

Aphids are a common cause of that on citrus new growth, so that's a reasonable starting guess. Do the insects look soft-bodied and pear-shaped, and are you seeing sticky residue or ants on the same shoots?
Actually there's no sticky residue and looking closer they're more oval and covered in a white waxy coating, not plain green like you'd expect from aphids.

That waxy white coating changes the picture — that description fits mealybugs rather than aphids, which have a similar sap-feeding habit but a distinctly different appearance and often hide in leaf axils and along stems more than aphids do. Mealybugs can be trickier to manage because their waxy coating protects them somewhat from water sprays, so physically wiping or brushing them off affected shoots, along with pruning out heavily infested growth, tends to help more directly than the water-spray approach that works reasonably well on true aphids.
My chili peppers have curling leaves and I can see small insects underneath, mostly green.
Curling leaves with small green insects clustered underneath is a classic aphid pattern on peppers. How badly curled are the leaves, and is it just a few plants or spreading through the plot?
Maybe a dozen plants out of fifty, leaves curled but not falling off yet.

That's a manageable level to catch it at. A strong jet of water aimed at the undersides of the curled leaves can dislodge a good number of aphids, and doing this every couple of days for the affected plants helps keep numbers down without any cost. Encouraging ladybirds and other natural predators by not spraying broadly also helps over the season.
What if the water spray isn't strong enough with my current setup?

If your sprayer or hose can't generate much pressure, a soapy water solution — a small amount of plain dish soap in water — sprayed directly onto the aphids can be effective at killing them on contact by breaking down their protective coating, without needing strong water pressure to physically dislodge them. Just avoid spraying it during the hottest part of the day, since soap solutions can sometimes stress leaves in strong sun.
My beans have dark sunken spots on the pods with a slightly pinkish centre when wet.

Dark, sunken spots on pods, especially with a pinkish tinge in wet conditions, is characteristic of anthracnose, a fungal disease that can also show on stems and leaves as similar dark lesions. Was this year particularly wet during pod formation?
Yes, we had a lot of rain right around when the pods were forming.

That timing is exactly when anthracnose does the most damage, since the fungus spreads readily in wet, humid conditions and pods are especially vulnerable while forming. For this crop, removing and destroying badly affected pods and plant debris after harvest, rather than leaving them in the field, reduces how much fungal material carries over to infect next season's crop. Using clean, disease-free seed for the next planting matters a lot too, since anthracnose can be carried on seed from an infected crop.
My wheat has orange-red powdery spots on the leaves and stems that rub off on my fingers.

Orange-red powdery pustules that rub off easily are the classic sign of rust disease in wheat, one of the more damaging fungal problems for the crop, especially in cooler, humid growing conditions. Is this appearing mainly on the leaves, or have you noticed it on the stems too?
Mostly leaves so far, a little starting on some stems.

Catching it while it's still mainly on the leaves is better than once it moves heavily into the stem, since stem rust tends to cause more severe yield loss. Rust spreads through windborne spores, so there's limited benefit to removing individual leaves at this scale — the more useful actions are checking whether your variety has any resistance rating against rust, since resistant varieties are the most effective long-term defence, and asking a local extension officer whether a fungicide application is currently recommended for the rust strain active in your area this season, since rust strains and their control needs shift over time.
My rice has diamond-shaped grey lesions with brown edges on the leaves.

Diamond or spindle-shaped lesions with a grey centre and darker brown border are a textbook description of rice blast, a fungal disease that can affect leaves early on and later move into the neck of the panicle, which is the more damaging stage since it can prevent grain filling. Is this showing on the leaves only so far, or have your rice plants headed out yet?
Still just leaves, no heading yet.

That's a better stage to be dealing with it at, since leaf blast alone, while it weakens the plant, doesn't directly destroy grain the way neck blast does later. Avoiding excess nitrogen fertiliser right now is worth knowing, since lush, heavily fertilised growth is more susceptible to blast, and keeping fields properly drained rather than waterlogged also reduces the humid conditions the fungus favours. If blast has been a recurring problem in your area, asking about blast-resistant rice varieties for your next planting is a longer-term way to reduce reliance on catching and treating it each season.
Some of my millet heads have turned into a black powdery mass instead of normal grain.

A black, powdery mass replacing normal grain in the head is typical of smut, a fungal disease that essentially replaces developing grain with fungal spores instead. Is this affecting most of the heads in the field, or just scattered individual plants?
Just scattered plants here and there, maybe one in every twenty or so.

At that scattered level, the most useful immediate step is removing and destroying the affected heads before they release spores, ideally by cutting and burning or burying them away from the field rather than leaving them to shatter and spread spores onto healthy plants or into the soil. Since smut spores can carry over on seed and in soil, using clean seed for your next planting and avoiding saving seed from this harvest, even from apparently unaffected plants in this field, reduces the chance of a bigger problem next season.
My avocados look fine when picked but develop black sunken patches a few days after harvest.

That delayed appearance of black, sunken patches after harvest is a common pattern with anthracnose in avocado, where the fungus can infect the fruit while still on the tree without showing symptoms until the fruit ripens and softens after picking. Are you harvesting fruit that's fallen or been in contact with the ground at all, or picking directly from the tree?
Mostly picked directly, though a few do fall and I pick those up too.

It's worth keeping those two separate — fallen fruit that's touched the ground picks up contamination more easily and is more likely to develop rot regardless of anthracnose, so selling or storing it separately from tree-picked fruit is a good practice. For the anthracnose itself, since infection often happens on the tree before harvest, removing dead twigs and fallen debris from under the tree reduces the amount of fungal material available to infect fruit, and handling fruit carefully to avoid bruising at harvest also matters, since damaged skin gives the fungus an easier entry point.
My mangoes look fine outside but when I cut them open there are maggots inside and the flesh is rotting around them.

That's consistent with fruit fly damage — the adult fly lays eggs just under the skin of the ripening fruit, and the maggots that hatch feed inside, with rot often following behind them as the flesh breaks down. Are you noticing tiny puncture marks or slight discolouration on the skin of otherwise normal-looking fruit?
Now that you mention it, yes, small dark dots on some fruit that I hadn't paid attention to before.

Those small dark dots are likely the egg-laying punctures. Since fruit flies are attracted to ripening fruit, harvesting mangoes a little earlier, at a mature-green stage rather than letting them ripen fully on the tree, reduces the window they're vulnerable. Collecting and destroying fallen or infested fruit promptly, rather than leaving it under the tree, also cuts down the population, since maggots that finish developing in fallen fruit go on to become the next generation of egg-laying flies. Fruit fly traps using a food-based lure hung in the tree can help monitor and reduce adult numbers as well.
My citrus leaves are blotchy yellow in an uneven pattern and the fruit is small and lopsided. What could cause that?

That combination — asymmetric yellow blotching on leaves along with small, lopsided, poorly coloured fruit — is consistent with citrus greening disease, a serious bacterial disease spread mainly by a small sap-feeding insect called the citrus psyllid, and also through infected budwood used for grafting. Do you know if psyllids have been seen in your area or on nearby citrus?
I'm not sure, I haven't specifically looked for them.

It's worth checking new growth on your trees closely, since psyllids are small and easy to miss. Unfortunately, there's no cure once a tree is infected, so management is mostly about limiting spread — removing severely affected trees, controlling psyllid populations on remaining trees, and only using certified disease-free planting material for any new trees, rather than grafting from a tree you're unsure about. A local citrus extension officer would be worth involving, since this disease is taken seriously as a regional threat and there may be area-wide monitoring already in place.
My sunflower heads are turning brown and mushy on the back, even before harvest.

Brown, mushy rot on the back of the head before harvest usually points to a fungal head rot, often encouraged by wet weather during and after flowering when the head is most vulnerable. Has it been unusually wet or humid around the time your sunflowers were flowering?
Yes, quite wet, more rain than usual during flowering.

That timing lines up well with how this problem typically develops. There isn't much to do for heads already rotting, but harvesting affected heads promptly rather than leaving them to fully dry in the field reduces further spoilage and the risk of the rot spreading spores to healthy heads nearby. For future seasons, wider plant spacing to improve airflow around the heads, and avoiding overhead watering during flowering if you irrigate, both reduce how long moisture sits on the vulnerable head tissue.
My sugarcane stalks have holes and when I cut one open there's a tunnel with a caterpillar inside.

A tunnel bored through the stalk with a caterpillar inside is typical of stem borer damage in sugarcane, which can significantly reduce both cane weight and sugar content since the tunnelling disrupts how the plant moves nutrients and water up the stalk. Is this showing up mainly in younger cane or across plants of different ages?
Mostly younger, recently established cane.

Younger cane is often more vulnerable since the stalks are still thin enough for larvae to bore through easily. Removing and destroying badly affected stalks helps reduce the population before larvae complete their lifecycle and produce more moths. Keeping the field free of old cane residue and volunteer regrowth after harvest also matters, since borers can carry over in leftover stalks between seasons rather than needing to reinfest from elsewhere each time.
My chilli pods have circular sunken spots with concentric rings, starting from the tip of the fruit.

Sunken, ringed spots starting from the fruit tip is a classic presentation of anthracnose on chilli, a fungal disease that tends to affect ripening or already-ripe fruit more than green fruit. Has the weather been particularly humid or wet lately?
