Yes, it's been quite humid, more than usual for this time of year.

That humidity is likely driving the outbreak, since anthracnose spreads readily in moist conditions. Removing and destroying affected pods rather than leaving them on the plant or the ground reduces the amount of fungal spore material available to spread to healthy fruit. Improving airflow by not overcrowding plants and avoiding wetting the fruit directly when watering also helps going forward, and picking chillies a bit earlier, before they're fully ripe, can reduce losses since anthracnose tends to hit riper fruit harder.
My carrots look fine above ground but when I pull them up there are tunnels through the roots.

Tunnelling through the root itself, without obvious damage to the leaves above ground, is typical of carrot root fly, whose larvae feed inside the root rather than on visible plant parts, which is why it's often only noticed at harvest. Is this affecting most of the crop or a smaller portion?
A decent portion, maybe a third of what I've pulled so far.

At a third affected, it's worth adjusting for the rest of the harvest and for next season both. For carrots still in the ground, harvesting a bit earlier than you might otherwise, rather than leaving them to grow larger, can reduce further tunnelling damage, since the flies have less time to lay eggs and larvae less time to develop. For future plantings, rotating carrots away from the same bed each season and avoiding leaving thinned or damaged carrot foliage lying around, since the odour can attract egg-laying flies, both help reduce how bad this gets next time.
My sweet potato leaves are small, distorted, and mottled, and the plants just aren't vigorous this season.

Small, distorted, mottled leaves with generally weak growth is a common description of sweet potato virus disease, which is actually a combination of two viruses working together and causes much more damage jointly than either does alone. It spreads mainly through whiteflies and aphids, and through using infected vines as planting material. Where did your planting vines for this season come from?
I took cuttings from my own field from last season, like I usually do.

That's likely how it's persisting, if last season's plants were already carrying the virus without you noticing milder symptoms — reusing vines from an infected crop just carries the problem forward each season. For future planting, sourcing clean vines, ideally from certified virus-free planting material or from a healthy-looking, vigorous crop with no history of these symptoms, is the main way to break the cycle, since there's no treatment for a plant once infected. Controlling the whiteflies and aphids that spread it between plants also helps limit how much it builds up within a season.
My passion fruit vines are wilting one at a time, starting with the older vines, and the leaves yellow before dropping.

Wilting that progresses through the vine gradually, often starting with older growth, and combined with yellowing before leaf drop, is consistent with fusarium wilt, a soil-borne fungal disease that blocks the plant's water-conducting tissue from within. Has this orchard had passion fruit growing in the same soil for several years?
Yes, going on six years now in the same spot.

That length of continuous cropping is a common setup for fusarium to build up, since the fungus persists in soil for a long time and increases with repeated planting of a susceptible crop in the same ground. There's no cure once a vine is infected, so removing and destroying wilted vines, including as much of the root system as practical, helps limit spread to neighbouring healthy vines. For replanting, grafting onto fusarium-resistant rootstock, where available, is the main long-term solution used in areas with this problem, since simply replanting susceptible vines in the same infected soil tends to run into the same issue again.
My export buyer rejected a batch of French beans for pesticide residue. What went wrong?

A residue rejection usually comes down to either using a product not approved for that export market, applying it too close to harvest, or applying more than the label's rate — export markets, especially in Europe, often test for very low residue thresholds that are stricter than what's required for local sale. Do you know which product was used and roughly how close to harvest it was applied?
I'm not totally sure, my worker handled the spraying and I didn't check the timing closely.

That gap is worth closing for future crops, since knowing exactly what was applied and when is essential for meeting export standards. Going forward, keeping a written spray record for every application, including the product, date, and who applied it, lets you calculate whether you're within the required pre-harvest interval before you pick and ship. It's also worth asking your export company or agrovet for their approved product list specifically for French beans destined for export, since it's often a narrower list than what's approved for general use, and checking that list before any spraying happens rather than after a rejection.
My Napier grass has basically stopped growing in this dry spell and I'm running out of feed for my cows.

Napier growth does slow drastically without rain, so a feed shortage in a dry spell is a common squeeze. Do you have any crop residues around, like maize stalks or bean straw, that could bridge the gap while you wait for rain?
Some maize stalks left from last harvest, not sure how much feed value they actually have.

Maize stalks have real feed value, though less than fresh Napier, especially if chopped up rather than fed whole, since that reduces wastage and makes them easier for the cows to eat. Combining them with anything else available, like any legume residues or even a bit of purchased feed if it's affordable, helps balance out what's a fairly low-quality feed on its own. For future dry spells, some farmers cut and store extra Napier as silage during the growing season specifically to have a reserve for exactly this kind of gap, which is worth considering once this dry spell passes.
My goat's belly is swollen on the left side and it seems uncomfortable, pawing at the ground.

A swollen left side of the belly along with obvious discomfort is consistent with bloat, a buildup of gas in the rumen that can become serious quickly if it isn't relieved. Do you know if it got into anything unusual recently, like a large amount of fresh legume forage or grain?
Actually yes, it got loose yesterday and ate a lot of fresh clover from a neighbour's patch.

That's a very typical trigger — a large amount of fresh, lush legume forage eaten quickly can produce bloat because it ferments fast in the rumen. This is worth treating as urgent rather than waiting to see if it passes, since severe bloat can become dangerous within hours. Keeping the goat moving gently rather than letting it lie down can sometimes help gas move, but getting a vet or experienced livestock handler to assess it properly is the safer path, since they can relieve bloat directly if it's serious, which isn't something to attempt without experience.
My cattle look thin and have rough coats even though they're grazing on decent pasture. Could it be worms?

Thin body condition with a rough, dull coat despite reasonable grazing is a common sign of internal parasites, so worms are a reasonable thing to suspect, though it's worth confirming rather than assuming, since other issues like poor mineral intake can look similar. Has it been a while since these animals were last dewormed or checked?
Honestly it's been a long time, maybe over a year.

That length of time without deworming does raise the likelihood that parasites are at least part of what's going on. Rather than guessing at which dewormer or how much to use, it's worth having a vet or livestock officer either do a faecal check to confirm worms are present, or at least advise on the right product for your specific cattle, since dosing depends on the animal's weight and the product's concentration, which varies by brand. Improving pasture rotation, so cattle aren't repeatedly grazing the same short grass where parasite larvae concentrate, also helps reduce reinfection once treated.
My chickens seem to be losing weight even though they're eating normally, is that worms?

Weight loss despite a normal appetite is one of the patterns that can point to intestinal worms in chickens, since the parasites are competing for the nutrition the bird is taking in. Have you noticed anything unusual in their droppings, or seen any worm segments directly?
Not that I've noticed, but I haven't looked closely either.

It's worth a closer look at their droppings over the next few days, since visible worm segments or unusual consistency can help confirm it before treating. Keeping the coop and run areas clean and dry, since damp, dirty conditions let worm eggs persist and get picked up again by the birds, helps regardless of whether it turns out to be worms. If you do decide to treat, ask your agrovet for a poultry dewormer appropriate for your flock and follow their guidance on amount and timing rather than estimating it yourself, since getting that wrong can be as much of a problem as the worms themselves.
My ducks have suddenly stopped laying eggs, from about ten a day down to almost none.

A sudden, sharp drop like that is worth investigating rather than assuming it's just a natural slowdown. Has anything changed recently — daylight hours, feed, water access, or any stress like a predator scare or a change in housing?
Now that I think about it, we did move them to a new pen about a week ago.

That timing is a strong candidate — a change in housing, even without obvious mistreatment, can stress ducks enough to disrupt laying for a period while they adjust. Ducks are generally sensitive to disruption in their routine and environment. Give them some time to settle into the new pen, make sure it has adequate shade, clean water, and feels secure from predators, and laying often recovers within a couple of weeks once they've adjusted, assuming nothing else changed at the same time like feed quality or daylight length dropping into a shorter season.
My rabbit keeps scratching its ears and there's a crusty brown buildup inside them.

Crusty brown buildup inside the ears combined with persistent scratching is a fairly classic sign of ear mites in rabbits, which can be quite uncomfortable and, left untreated, can progress to more serious ear infections. Is it one ear or both, and does the rabbit seem to be shaking its head a lot?
Both ears, and yes, a lot of head shaking.

Both ears affected with a lot of head shaking suggests this has been going on for a bit and is worth treating rather than waiting out. It's best handled by a vet or someone experienced with rabbits, since ear mites are usually treated with a specific medication rather than home remedies, and rabbit ears are sensitive enough that cleaning them incorrectly can cause more harm than good. In the meantime, avoid trying to scrape out the crusting yourself, since that can be painful and cause bleeding if the skin underneath is already irritated.
I found webbing and tunnels through the wax comb in one of my hive boxes that wasn't in use.

Webbing and tunnelling through unused comb is a classic sign of wax moth, which target stored or unused comb rather than comb that's actively being tended by a strong colony of bees. Was this box empty and stored away from an active colony, or attached to a hive that still has bees in it?
It was stored in a shed, not attached to any active hive.

That's exactly the situation wax moths exploit, since unguarded comb has no bees to defend it. For the affected comb, it's usually best to remove and melt down badly damaged wax rather than trying to save it, since the moth larvae can have tunnelled through extensively even where damage isn't fully obvious. Going forward, storing empty comb in a way that keeps moths out — sealed containers, or freezing comb briefly before storage to kill any eggs already present — helps prevent this happening to your next batch of spare boxes.
A lot of my tilapia died overnight, no visible marks, just floating at the surface.

Sudden overnight deaths with no visible injury, especially fish found at the surface, often points to oxygen depletion in the pond, which tends to be worst in the early morning after oxygen has been used up overnight by fish, plants, and decomposing matter, with no sunlight yet to let algae replenish it through photosynthesis. Has the pond had a lot of algae or plant growth lately, or any recent heavy rain or hot, still weather?
Actually yes, quite a green pond the last couple of weeks and it's been very hot and calm.

That combination — heavy algae growth plus hot, still weather — is a strong risk factor for exactly this kind of overnight oxygen crash, since a large algae population consumes a lot of oxygen at night and dying algae decomposing adds to the drain. Reducing excess nutrients going into the pond, such as from overfeeding or manure runoff, helps control algae levels going forward. In the shorter term, some form of aeration, even simply splashing or paddling water to mix in oxygen during a still, hot spell, can help reduce the risk on nights when conditions look similar to what led to this loss.
My fish pond water has turned bright green almost overnight, is that a problem?

A sudden, bright green colour usually means an algae bloom, which isn't automatically catastrophic but is worth watching closely, since a heavy bloom followed by an algae die-off can crash oxygen levels in the pond quite suddenly, especially overnight. Do you know what might have triggered it — recent feeding changes, fertiliser runoff, or a stretch of sunny, warm weather?
We did increase feeding recently to try to grow the fish faster.

That's a common trigger — excess feed that isn't eaten breaks down and releases nutrients that algae use to grow rapidly. Cutting back feeding to what the fish will actually consume within a few minutes, rather than feeding more than they need, usually helps bring the bloom back under control over time. It's worth watching the fish closely in the mornings for now, since that's when oxygen is lowest, and if you see fish gasping at the surface, that's a sign the bloom has tipped into a more urgent oxygen problem needing more immediate action.
How do I actually get my soil tested, is that something available to smallholders or only big farms?

Soil testing is generally available to smallholders too, not just larger operations, though access depends on what's near you. Government agricultural extension offices often offer it directly or can direct you to a lab, and some agricultural universities or cooperatives also run testing services, sometimes at a lower cost for smallholder samples. Have you been in touch with your local extension office before for anything else?
Not really, I've mostly just relied on advice from other farmers and the agrovet.

That's a reasonable starting network, but for something as specific as a soil test, the extension office is worth a direct visit, since they'll be able to tell you the nearest lab, roughly what it costs, and how to take a proper sample, which matters for getting a result that actually reflects your field rather than one patch of it. It's a worthwhile one-time or occasional expense, since decisions like liming or specific fertiliser choices work much better when based on an actual test rather than general advice that wasn't tailored to your soil.
My maize has a white or pale striping between the veins on the newer leaves, but the veins themselves stay green.

Pale striping between green veins, especially on newer growth, is a pattern often linked to zinc deficiency, which can show up even in soils that otherwise have adequate major nutrients, particularly in soils that are alkaline or have had heavy phosphorus application, since high phosphorus can interfere with zinc uptake. Have you been applying phosphorus fertiliser heavily in recent seasons?
Yes, fairly heavily, we've been pushing for higher yields with more DAP each season.

That fits — a heavy, sustained phosphorus programme without matching attention to micronutrients like zinc can tip a soil toward zinc deficiency over time, even if zinc levels were adequate before. A zinc-containing fertiliser or foliar zinc application can correct it for the current crop, and going forward it's worth having your soil tested for micronutrients as well as the major ones, since correcting zinc without addressing the underlying phosphorus-zinc imbalance could mean this recurs each season you push phosphorus hard.
My banana leaves are yellowing between the veins on the older leaves, but the veins stay dark green, kind of a herringbone pattern.

That herringbone pattern — yellowing between veins while the veins themselves stay green, especially on older leaves — is a fairly classic sign of magnesium deficiency, which shows on older leaves first because the plant moves what magnesium it has toward newer growth when supply is short. Has this orchard had heavy potassium fertiliser use, since high potassium can interfere with how the plant takes up magnesium?
Yes actually, we've been applying quite a bit of potassium to boost bunch size.

That's a likely contributor — heavy potassium application can create a magnesium shortage even in soil that has reasonable magnesium, simply because the plant takes up the more abundant nutrient preferentially. Applying a magnesium-containing fertiliser, or using a dolomitic lime if your soil could also use a pH adjustment, helps correct the deficiency directly, and going forward, balancing potassium applications with occasional magnesium rather than pushing potassium alone tends to prevent this imbalance from recurring.
My irrigation water has gotten saltier over the years as my borehole has aged. Should I change what I'm growing?

That's a reasonable thing to consider, since crops vary quite a bit in how much salt stress they can tolerate before yield suffers. Do you know roughly how salty the water has become, or is this based on general observation like crop performance declining?
Mostly based on the crops doing worse, especially my lettuce and beans, I haven't had the water tested.

Lettuce and beans are both on the more salt-sensitive side, so struggling crops there is consistent with rising salinity even without a specific number. Getting the water actually tested would help confirm the level and guide which crops are realistic going forward, since some crops like certain barley or sorghum varieties tolerate salinity much better than sensitive vegetables. In the meantime, watering with enough volume to flush salts below the root zone rather than just wetting the surface, where your water supply allows it, can help sensitive crops cope a bit better even without switching entirely.
Heavy rain damaged part of my terrace wall on the hillside plot. Do I need to rebuild the whole thing?

Not necessarily the whole terrace — it depends on how much of the wall or bank actually failed versus just eroded a bit at the surface. Is the damage a full collapse of the wall in one section, or more like erosion wearing down the face of it?
One section did fully collapse, maybe a few metres of it, the rest looks okay.

For a localised collapse like that, repairing just that section, rather than reconstructing the whole terrace, is usually sufficient, as long as you address whatever caused that specific section to fail — often it's water concentrating there because of a low point or a channel that formed above it. Before rebuilding, it's worth digging a small diversion or checking that water isn't still funnelling to that same spot, since rebuilding without fixing the underlying water flow often means the same section fails again in the next heavy rain.
What does planting on the contour actually mean, and is it different from just planting in straight rows?

Planting on the contour means following the natural, level curve of the land as it wraps around a slope, rather than planting in straight rows that might run up and down a hill regardless of its shape. The point is that rows running along the contour are all at roughly the same elevation, so water moving across the slope meets a series of small barriers, your crop rows and the ridges between them, that slow it down rather than a smooth channel running straight downhill. Do you have much slope on your land, or is it fairly flat?
There's a noticeable slope, maybe not steep, but definitely not flat.

Even a gentle slope benefits from contour planting, since water still picks up speed and starts carrying soil away on a slope that doesn't look dramatically steep. Marking out the contour lines properly, often done with a simple line level or an A-frame tool if you don't have surveying equipment, is worth doing once properly rather than guessing, since rows that drift even slightly off the true contour create low points where water concentrates and can start new erosion channels.
My neighbour plants Grevillea trees in lines through his maize field. What's the actual benefit of that?

Grevillea is commonly used in agroforestry alongside crops like maize because it has a relatively narrow, deep root system compared to many trees, which means it competes less with the shallower-rooted crop for water and nutrients near the surface than a wider-rooting tree would. Beyond that, it provides useful timber and firewood over time, some shade and wind protection, and leaf litter that adds organic matter to the soil. Is your interest mainly in the soil benefit, or more about getting wood from the same land you're already cropping?
Mostly the wood, honestly, firewood is getting harder to find nearby.

That's a very practical reason on its own, and Grevillea is a reasonable choice for it, since it grows relatively quickly and coppices well, meaning you can cut it back and it regrows rather than needing full replanting each time you harvest wood. Planting it in lines along field boundaries or between crop strips, rather than scattered randomly, makes it easier to manage the shade it casts on your maize, since even a root system that competes less can still shade nearby crop rows if trees are left to grow tall and close together.
Strong winds keep drying out my soil and blowing away topsoil in the dry season. Would a windbreak actually help?

Yes, a well-placed windbreak can help meaningfully with both problems, since slowing wind speed at ground level reduces both the moisture loss from evaporation and the physical lifting of loose, dry topsoil. Do you know the direction the strong winds mainly come from during your dry season?
Mostly from one direction, I'd say roughly the same direction each year.

That consistency makes planning a windbreak more straightforward — planting a line of trees or shrubs perpendicular to that prevailing wind direction, upwind of the area you're most trying to protect, gives you the most benefit for the fewest plants. It takes a few years for a planted windbreak to grow tall and dense enough to meaningfully slow wind, so it's more of a medium-term investment than an immediate fix, but combining it with mulching or other ground cover in the meantime protects the soil while the windbreak establishes.
Is there a way to treat my vegetable seeds for disease without buying a chemical seed treatment?

Yes, hot water seed treatment is a non-chemical option used for a number of vegetable seeds to reduce seed-borne disease, working by killing pathogens on or in the seed coat using controlled heat before the heat gets high enough to damage the seed itself. It requires care with both temperature and timing, since too hot or too long can kill the seed's ability to germinate, and too mild won't kill the pathogens effectively. Which vegetable are you planning to treat this way?
Cabbage seed, I've had some seed-borne disease issues in past seasons.

Cabbage and related brassica seed are commonly treated this way for exactly that reason. Since getting the water temperature and soaking time precisely right matters a lot for this to work without damaging the seed, it's worth getting the specific temperature and duration from a seed supplier or extension officer familiar with cabbage seed treatment rather than guessing, since the margin for error is fairly narrow and ruined seed viability would cost you more than the problem you were trying to solve.
Are those hermetic storage bags for grain actually worth the extra cost compared to ordinary sacks?

For many smallholders they are, mainly because they remove the need for chemical grain protectants and can significantly cut losses from insect pests like weevils and the larger grain borer, since the sealed environment starves insects of the oxygen they need rather than relying on a pesticide. The extra upfront cost is the main downside. How much grain are you typically storing, and have you had ongoing pest losses with your current sacks?
A fair amount, maybe fifteen bags a season, and yes, we usually lose a noticeable portion to weevils by the time we sell.

With losses at that scale each season, hermetic bags are quite likely to pay for themselves over a season or two, since preventing even a modest percentage of loss on fifteen bags can outweigh the price difference from ordinary sacks. They're also reusable across multiple seasons if handled carefully, which improves the value further over time compared to a one-season cost. It's worth checking with local suppliers on price, since it can vary, and comparing that against roughly what your typical weevil losses have cost you in past seasons.
Is it worth investing in drying my mangoes to sell as dried fruit instead of selling them fresh?

It can be worth it, particularly because dried mango has a much longer shelf life than fresh fruit, which matters a lot during your mango season's glut period when fresh prices often crash from oversupply. Do you have a solar dryer or other drying setup already, or would this mean starting from scratch?
Starting from scratch, I'd need to figure out drying and figure out where to sell dried mango too.

Starting from scratch means factoring in both the equipment cost and the time to find a reliable market before counting on this as income, which makes it more of a medium-term project than an immediate solution for this season's harvest. A basic solar dryer is a relatively low-cost way to start rather than an electric dehydrator, and it's worth testing with a small batch first to work out your process and find buyers, whether through local markets, shops, or a farmer group that might already have distribution, before committing bigger volumes of fruit and time to it.
I'm planning to rotate onions with beans next season since they're both legumes, for the nitrogen benefit.

I want to correct one part of that — onions aren't actually legumes, they're in the allium family along with garlic and leeks, so they don't fix nitrogen the way beans do. That doesn't mean rotating onions and beans is a bad idea though, it can still work well for other reasons, like breaking pest and disease cycles that build up when the same crop family is grown repeatedly. You'd just want to think of the nitrogen benefit as something beans contribute to the soil for whatever follows them, rather than a benefit onions bring in return.
Oh okay, so should beans come before onions in the rotation then, to pass on that nitrogen?

Yes, that's the more useful order — planting beans first lets them build up nitrogen in the soil through their root nodules over that season, and then planting onions afterward lets them benefit from that residual nitrogen, along with whatever crop residue is worked back into the soil. Onions followed by beans wouldn't give you that same benefit, since onions aren't adding anything back for the beans to use.
I bought Newcastle vaccine and left it in a warm bag for a few hours before using it, but it should still work fine since it's just a liquid, right?

Actually, that's likely to be a problem rather than a minor detail — most Newcastle disease vaccines are live and need to stay cold to remain effective, and a few hours in a warm bag can significantly weaken or destroy that effectiveness even though the liquid still looks completely normal. There's no way to tell just by looking whether it's still potent. If you're not confident it stayed properly cold the whole time, it's safer to treat this batch as unreliable and get a fresh one that's been kept cold throughout, rather than vaccinate your flock and assume it worked, since a failed vaccination that you believe succeeded leaves the flock exposed without you realising it.
That's disappointing, is there any way to test if it still works before using it on the whole flock?

There isn't a practical way to test vaccine potency yourself at home — that requires laboratory conditions rather than anything you could check on the farm. Given the flock's protection is what's at stake, it's not worth gambling on a batch with an uncertain cold chain; getting a replacement and being more deliberate about keeping it cold from purchase to use, such as carrying it in a cool box with ice rather than a normal bag, is the more reliable path forward.
My tomato seedlings have been in the nursery for two months now, is it too late to transplant them?

Two months in the nursery is considerably longer than the usual four to six weeks before tomato seedlings are normally ready to transplant, so they may have become overgrown, root-bound, or stressed in their containers, which can affect how well they establish once moved. How do they actually look right now — still healthy and green, or getting leggy, yellowing, or root-bound in their containers?
Actually I think I miscounted, checking my notes it's been about five weeks, not two months, sorry.

That's a much more typical timeframe, so no need to worry about the overgrown-seedling concerns I raised — five weeks is within the normal window for tomato seedlings to be ready for transplanting. As long as they look reasonably sturdy with a few true leaves and aren't obviously wilting or yellowing, this is a fine time to move them out, and there's no real downside to getting them into the field now rather than waiting further, since holding seedlings in small containers past their ready stage is more the concern than transplanting at five weeks.
